entries.summary: The Kotlin Toolchain helps you build and ship multiplatform apps faster, with less setup and configuration.
entries.text: The Kotlin Toolchain helps you build and ship multiplatform apps faster, with less setup and configuration. Its CLI provides a unified workflow for building, running, testing, and publishing apps for Android, iOS, desktop, and web, whether you’re developing with AI agents or writing code yourself. Kotlin Toolchain 0.14 makes it easier to publish iOS apps to TestFlight and brings improvements to agentic development workflows, along with several other enhancements. Install Kotlin Toolchain Or try this prompt in your favorite agent: Create a new Kotlin Multiplatform app for Android, iOS, desktop, and web with the Kotlin Toolchain CLI (https://kotlin-toolchain.org/latest). Copy To access the latest Kotlin Toolchain features from your IDE, use IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.4 (or newer) or Android Studio Rabbit 1 | 2026.2.1 (or newer). Make sure the latest version of the Kotlin Toolchain plugin is installed. iOS application publishing You can now publish iOS apps using the kotlin publish testflight command. This launches an easy publishing flow that guides you through most of the setup and steps required to publish a new application to TestFlight for the first time. After the first publication, you can publish updates automatically using the same command. The command will ask for an App Store Connect access token (Apple Developer Program membership is required, as usual), which is a standard way to authorize automations to publish applications in App Store Connect. entries.summary: The Kotlin Multiplatform Contest is back! Students and recent graduates, turn your idea into a cross-platform project with Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP).
entries.text: The Kotlin Multiplatform Contest is back! Students and recent graduates, turn your idea into a cross-platform project with Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP). The authors of the top three projects will each win a trip to KotlinConf 2027 in Kraków, Poland, with conference tickets, travel, and accommodation covered by the Kotlin Foundation. Authors of all other valid entries will receive Kotlin souvenirs. Submissions are open until December 7, 2026. Join the contest Your project can be a game, a developer utility, a productivity app, an experiment with AI, or something entirely different. It needs to be created specifically for the contest, use KMP, and run on at least two platforms. Target Android, iOS, desktop, web, backend, or beyond. Last year, we received 88 submissions, with 76 eligible entries from more than 30 countries. Participants built everything from AI-powered learning tools to social-impact projects and accessibility apps. We can’t wait to see what you build this year! Important dates Submission deadline: December 7, 2026, 23:59 CET Winners announced: December 21, 2026 KotlinConf 2027: April 22–23, 2027, Kraków, Poland For the official rules on eligibility, submission, and prize conditions, see here. Have questions or need help? Join the KMP Contest Slack channel to ask questions, follow contest updates, and connect with other participants and Kotlin experts. entries.summary: Google Summer of Code 2026 has wrapped up! This was the Kotlin Foundation’s fourth year participating in GSoC, bringing new contributors into the Kotlin open-source ecosystem through hands-on projects and mentorship.
entries.text: Google Summer of Code 2026 has wrapped up! This was the Kotlin Foundation’s fourth year participating in GSoC, bringing new contributors into the Kotlin open-source ecosystem through hands-on projects and mentorship. This year, two projects successfully reached completion, tackling two areas of the ecosystem: improving recursion support in the Kotlin/Wasm backend and building a global picture of where Kotlin is taught. Congratulations to Ayako Hayasaka and Mark Seif Khalil, and a huge thank-you to our mentors for supporting them throughout the program! Here’s more on what they accomplished. Tail call support in the Kotlin/Wasm backend Contributor: Ayako Hayasaka Mentor: Charlie Zhang (JetBrains) Ayako’s project added support for WebAssembly tail-call instructions to the Kotlin/Wasm backend. The compiler can now detect calls in tail position and emit return_call or return_call_ref, helping recursive Kotlin/Wasm programs avoid increasing the call stack. In Ayako’s benchmarks, several recursive patterns became 1.7–4.3x faster at a recursion depth of 10,000. At a depth of one million, the same programs crashed without tail calls and completed successfully with them. Testing the change on real-world projects also revealed an unexpected performance regression in V8. entries.summary: The KotlinConf 2027 Call for Papers is now open! We invite developers from across the Kotlin community to bring their ideas, experiences, and expertise to the stage in Kraków.
entries.text: The KotlinConf 2027 Call for Papers is now open! We invite developers from across the Kotlin community to bring their ideas, experiences, and expertise to the stage in Kraków. Do you have a Kotlin lesson or discovery that could help other developers? Perhaps you solved a difficult technical problem, introduced Kotlin into an existing codebase, built something unexpected, or learned valuable lessons from an approach that did not go according to plan. That experience could become a KotlinConf talk. Submit your proposal However, turning an idea into a convincing conference proposal can be challenging, especially if you’ve never submitted one before. How do you know whether your experience is worth sharing? What do reviewers notice first? How detailed should your abstract be? And how can you make a familiar topic stand out? To help you prepare your submission, we asked Kotlin developers, developer advocates, experienced speakers, and KotlinConf program committee members what makes a strong proposal. Alongside practical advice for shaping your title, abstract, and takeaways, we have added a new section answering an especially important question: What do reviewers notice first when they open a proposal? First-time speaker? Submit your idea anyway! It’s easy to assume that a KotlinConf talk must begin with a groundbreaking discovery, a major production system, or years of speaking experience. entries.text: This article was written by an external contributor. Aniket Bhattacharyea Aniket is a Mathematics postgraduate who has a passion for computers and software. He likes to explore various areas related to coding and works as a web developer using Ruby on Rails and Next.JS. Website Yuri Geronimus’s four-year-old son once asked him what his job was. Yuri told him he writes books: books that describe what he wants to change in the physical world. His son didn’t fully get it. Neither would most engineers: if you understand the words in your application code, you build good systems. If you don’t, you build bugs. That’s the spine of Yuri Geronimus’s KotlinConf 2026 talk, “Kotlin as a Safety Net: Type-Driven Reliability in the Finance Industry”. Yuri is an architect at Verifone, where he works across payment terminals, gateways, and the systems that connect them to banks and regulators in the EMEA region. His method, in one line: write code in the exact words of the regulator or card network specs, and let the compiler enforce it. Enforce not by discipline, but by the compiler. entries.summary: The Kotlin Toolchain is a unified entry point into Kotlin. It lets you build JVM, Android, iOS, multiplatform, and server-side applications with a simple declarative configuration.
entries.text: The Kotlin Toolchain is a unified entry point into Kotlin. It lets you build JVM, Android, iOS, multiplatform, and server-side applications with a simple declarative configuration. With the release of v0.13, we now recommend the Kotlin Toolchain for most new Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) projects. Earlier this year, we promoted the Kotlin Toolchain to Alpha. Since then, our Slack channels and issue tracker have been very active. So many of you in the community have joined us to create a great build experience for Kotlin. Thank you – your continuous feedback helped us get here! Not using the Kotlin Toolchain yet? Experience automated environment setup and an intuitive CLI that works well with your AI agents. Install Kotlin Toolchain To access the latest Kotlin Toolchain features from your IDE, use IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2.3, Android Studio Rabbit 1 | 2026.2.1 (or newer). Make sure the latest version of the Kotlin Toolchain plugin is installed. How the Kotlin Toolchain simplifies getting started Getting started with Kotlin Multiplatform often means working with unfamiliar platforms. Android developers might be discovering iOS for the first time, while other teams are expanding to web or desktop. Every platform comes with its own tools to install and build configurations to understand. The Kotlin Toolchain changes that. entries.summary: Starting with IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3 and Android Studio Rabbit 2 | 2026.2.2, we’re discontinuing Swift language IDE features in the Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) plugin.
entries.text: Starting with IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3 and Android Studio Rabbit 2 | 2026.2.2, we’re discontinuing Swift language IDE features in the Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) plugin. This includes editing, syntax highlighting, and navigation within Swift files and between Swift and Kotlin. Running iOS applications and debugging Kotlin code on iOS will remain fully supported. Kotlin/Native functionality, such as Swift Export and importing Swift packages into Kotlin projects, is not affected. The existing Swift functionality will remain available in earlier versions of IntelliJ IDEA, Android Studio, and the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin, though these older versions will not receive further updates. Background We originally developed Swift support for AppCode (our since-discontinued iOS IDE) and for working directly with Xcode projects. This technology was later adapted for Fleet’s polyglot capabilities and, most recently, for working with mixed Kotlin–Swift codebases using the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin. While analyzing feature adoption, we found that active usage was limited and steadily declining. Our telemetry and user research showed that most iOS developers working on KMP projects prefer using Xcode for Swift development, while teams that primarily work in the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin increasingly use Kotlin and Compose Multiplatform. entries.title: Discontinuing Swift Language IDE Support in the Kotlin Multiplatform Plugin

entries.summary: We are working on extensions to our companions mechanism to unlock new code patterns and improve interoperability across different platforms.
entries.text: We are working on extensions to our companions mechanism to unlock new code patterns and improve interoperability across different platforms. This post outlines these new features and provides preliminary guidance on migration. Companion blocks and extensions Many programming languages provide a notion of class or type members – functionality that does not belong to each particular value of a class, but to the class itself. Constants, utilities, and factory methods are often in this group. val v1 = Vector(1.0, 2.0) // a regular vector val v2 = Vector.ZERO // the constant zero vector val v3 = Vector.unit(angle = PI / 2) // unit vector with an angle Previously, companion objects were used to define these members. From Kotlin 2.5.0 on, you can also use an experimental companion block, which is very close syntactically, but with profound changes in compilation. data class Vector(val x: Double, val y: Double) { companion { val ZERO = Vector(0.0, 0.0) } } In fact, these members may not be defined directly on the class itself. You can also use an experimental companion extension to declare new class members in a type, even if you don’t control them. companion fun Vector.unit(angle: Double) = Vector(cos(angle), sin(angle)) The design of companion blocks and extensions overcomes the limitations imposed by companion objects. entries.summary: In 2026, Kotlin turned fifteen. Over those fifteen years, Kotlin has built a mature ecosystem, been adopted by companies around the world, and established a large and active developer community.
entries.text: In 2026, Kotlin turned fifteen. Over those fifteen years, Kotlin has built a mature ecosystem, been adopted by companies around the world, and established a large and active developer community. Fifteen years is long enough to understand which technology trends lasted and which didn’t. This report looks back at Kotlin’s first fifteen years to see what they reveal about how the language matured, while answering questions like: “Is Kotlin here to stay?”, “Can Kotlin scale across platforms?”, and “How does Kotlin fit into the AI era?” View Report State of Kotlin in 2026 Today, developers worldwide use Kotlin across a diverse range of applications, including mobile, backend, and multiplatform. The language is also finding its place in the rapidly evolving AI space, where Kotlin’s strengths, like static typing, null safety, and coroutines, take on new relevance. Kotlin is actively participating in the shift toward AI-assisted development: Among surveyed Kotlin developers, 93% use at least one AI coding tool, while 81% already use or are likely to try AI coding agents. An equal share – 81% – say that AI-generated Kotlin code is fully correct or requires only minor fixes. The State of Kotlin in 2026 report combines data from JetBrains research with independent industry data and real-world adoption evidence. entries.summary: The current compilation approach to Kotlin Multiplatform projects works, but sometimes can lead to unexpected or hard-to-predict behavior.
entries.text: The current compilation approach to Kotlin Multiplatform projects works, but sometimes can lead to unexpected or hard-to-predict behavior. For example: The IDE analysis disagrees with the compiler on an overload, type inference, or whether the code should compile at all – with the IDE being stricter than the compiler. Your commonTest code can unexpectedly call something from a platform source set, breaking your assumptions. With Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta1, we introduced an optional “separate compilation” approach to KMP that solves both problems: make the compilation results consistent with IDE analysis, and point more consistently to problematic calls of library code from common source sets. As a bonus, this approach enables us to implement incremental compilation for common source sets. The separate compilation feature is Experimental and disabled by default. To opt in, add the following compiler option to your gradle.properties file (note the known issues): kotlin.kmp.separateCompilation=true Let’s look closer at the problem and the solution. How multiplatform declarations are resolved within a module Within a module, multiplatform code performs predictably: // jvmMain fun foo() {} // commonMain fun test() { foo() // Unresolved reference in IDE and during compilation } The compiler and the IDE agree: The code in commonMain is also compiled to other platforms, for example, to Kotlin/JS, and there might not be a fun foo() declaration in jsMain. entries.summary: The Kotlin 2.4.20 release is out! Here are the main highlights: For the complete list of changes, see What’s new in Kotlin 2.4.20 or the release notes on GitHub.
entries.text: The Kotlin 2.4.20 release is out! Here are the main highlights: Standard library: Support for coroutine stack trace recovery, new functions for checking equality and uniqueness of collection elements, and new overloads for kotlin.test assertion functions. Kotlin/Native: New Swift export features, improved incremental compilation, and automatically generated Package.swift files for SwiftPM dependencies. Kotlin/Wasm: Changes to top-level require() calls in @JsFun declarations, improved companion object initialization order, and support for Wasmtime in the Kotlin Gradle plugin. Kotlin/JS: A new DSL for browser testing, support for exporting suspend lambdas as async functions, and improved exportability of data classes. Gradle: Support for Gradle 9.7.0 and improved reporting in the Problems API. Build tools API: Support for new targets: Kotlin/JS, Kotlin/Wasm, and Kotlin metadata. Kotlin compiler: The `kotlinr` runner command and a separate native image. For the complete list of changes, see What’s new in Kotlin 2.4.20 or the release notes on GitHub. How to install Kotlin 2.4.20 The latest version of Kotlin is included in the latest versions of IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio. To update to the new Kotlin version, make sure your IDE is updated to the latest version and change the Kotlin version to 2.4.20 in your build scripts.
